title: Bitmask DP
tagline: Encode a subset as the bits of an integer — DP over states of small sets.

intuition.analogy: Tracking which of n chores are done with a row of light switches. The on/off pattern is a binary number, so 'which subset is finished' becomes a single integer you can use as a DP index.
paragraphs: When n is small (≤ ~20), a subset of n items can be represented by an n-bit integer mask — bit i set means item i is included. This lets you DP over all 2^n subsets using an array indexed by the mask.

It shines for problems like the Travelling Salesman, assignment, and 'cover all tasks' where the state must remember exactly which elements have been used. dp[mask][i] often means 'minimum cost to have visited the set mask, currently at i'.

Bit tricks make transitions fast: test bit (mask >> i & 1), set bit (mask | 1<<i), iterate submasks, and use __builtin_popcount for set size. The exponential factor is unavoidable but tolerable for small n.
intuition.keyIdea: A subset is just an integer's bits; DP indexed by mask remembers which elements are used.

steps.title: Encode the state
steps.detail: mask = which elements are chosen/visited. Add extra dimensions (like current node) as needed.

steps.title: Order by increasing mask
steps.detail: A mask depends on masks with fewer bits, so iterating masks in increasing numeric order respects dependencies.

steps.title: Transition with bit ops
steps.detail: Extend the state by setting an unset bit: new = mask | (1<<j), updating dp[new] from dp[mask].

problems.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

approach: Each element is either used or not — a subset, encoded as a bitmask. dp[mask] = the amount filled in the current bucket (mod target) when exactly the elements in mask are placed.

If the total isn't divisible by k, or any element exceeds target, it's impossible. Otherwise add an unused element only if it keeps the current bucket <= target; reaching the full mask with remainder 0 means success.

approach: State is (current node, set of visited nodes as a bitmask). We want the shortest walk whose mask becomes all-ones.
BFS over these states (edges are unweighted) starting from every node with only itself visited; the first time any state reaches the full mask gives the answer.

problems.title: Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats
problems.statement: Count assignments of hats to people.
problems.hint: DP over a mask of assigned people.

approach: There are at most 10 people but 40 hats, so make people the bitmask (2^10) and iterate over hats.
dp[mask] = ways to assign hats so the people in mask have hats. For each hat, optionally give it to one person who likes it: dp'[mask | 1<<p] += dp[mask]. Answer is dp[fullPeople].

problems.title: Maximum Students Taking Exam
problems.statement: Seat max students with no cheating adjacency.
problems.hint: Row-by-row DP over seat masks; validate against the previous row.

approach: Process the grid row by row; each row's seating is a bitmask. A valid row mask uses only good seats and has no two horizontally adjacent students.

A row mask is compatible with the previous row's mask if there are no upper-left/upper-right conflicts: (mask & prev<<1)==0 and (mask & prev>>1)==0. DP keeps the max students over compatible transitions.

approach: Held-Karp: dp[mask][i] = minimum cost of a path that visits exactly the nodes in mask and ends at i.
Transition from dp[mask][i] to dp[mask | 1<<j][j] adding dist[i][j]. The answer is the minimum dp[full][i] over all endpoints i (a Hamiltonian path).
